title: Payload-aware batch fragmentation performance notes
content:
Summary:

This note captures an investigation into a recurring tail-latency and throughput regression we’ve observed on mixed workloads with variable prompt payloads (structured tool calls + long chat histories). The regression is especially visible on long-context runs (>= 16k) across Llama-2, Mistral, and Qwen families and gets amplified when MoE routing is enabled. The core phenomenon: dynamic per-request effective sequence length and routing decisions cause batch fragmentation, increasing kernel launch overheads, KV cache churn, and unaffordable synchronization at the router stage.

Why this matters:
- SLOs: p95/p99 latency spikes cause degraded UX for interactive features.
- Cost: reduced GPU token/s and increased 99s latency increase tail cost dramatically for Dedicated pools.
- Predictability: customers who pin model version + long-history workloads see inconsistent throughput.

Testbed and workload details:
- Hardware: A100 80GB and MI250X nodes (single card runs for deterministic profiling).
- Models: Llama-2-70b (fp16), Mistral-34b (q4f16), Qwen-34b (fp16), MoE experiment: hybrid-architecture with 64 experts, top-2 gating.
- Context: long-history chat traces synthesized from production traces: 50% short prompts (<=128 tokens), 30% medium (512-2048), 20% long (8k-32k).
- Arrival pattern: poisson with bursts (peak concurrency ~48 requests/card).
- Serving runtime flags: routing enabled, kv-prefix-cache on, dynamic-batching on, prefetch-experts disabled for baseline.

Profiling artifacts (high-level):
- Median per-token GPU throughput drop of 18–26% once batch fragmentation > 30% (batch fragmentation metric defined below).
- p99 latency increases from ~420ms to 1.1s in the worst long-context+MoE mix on A100.
- Flamegraphs show increased idle gaps between attention kernels and router sync points; kernel occupancy for attention drops by ~12% at fragmentation peaks.
- NVProf/TorchProfiler traces show additional small kernels (indexing, gather/scatter) increasing total kernel count per step by 40–70%, amplifying launch overheads.

Definitions and metrics used:
- effective_seq_len: per-request sequence length after prefix concatenation and tokenization.
- fragmentation_ratio = 1 - (coalesced_tokens / sum(effective_seq_len across batch)). Coalesced_tokens is token count actually placed into contiguous GPU buffers without padding/gap-induced extra kernel calls.
- router_sync_wait: cumulative time waiting on router consensus barriers (MoE) per step.

Key observations and root causes:
1) Payload heterogeneity causes internal micro-batches: when requests within a batch have widely different effective_seq_len, the runtime splits execution into multiple partial pipelines (fragmentation). This increases kernel launches and memory traffic.

2) MoE gating magnifies fragmentation: because gating chooses different expert sets per request, the implementation currently serializes some expert dispatches and introduces router_sync_wait. When combined with sequence-length variability, some requests finish earlier and leave slots idle while the router waits for stragglers.

3) KV cache and prefetch inefficiencies: long-context requests touch large KV shards; fragmentation increases the working set churn because partial coalescing changes placement patterns and increases cache misses. Observed KV hit-rate drop of 8–14% in fragmented runs.

4) Small indexing kernels become dominant: gather/scatter and index-lUT kernels (for routing and expert dispatch) are short but frequent. Increased kernel count (even if each is micro) hurts throughput due to launch overhead and SM scheduler churn, especially on GPUs with lower kernel launch throughput.

Experiments run (selected):
A. Baseline (no routing): dynamic-batching with homogeneous token lengths (control).
B. Heterogeneous payloads, routing disabled: fragmentation metric ~22%, throughput down 10% vs A.
C. Heterogeneous payloads, routing enabled (top-2, 64 experts), prefetch off: fragmentation ~46%, p99 up 2.5x vs A. router_sync_wait accounts for ~28% of step time.
D. Same as C but with prefetch-experts on (speculative dispatch): fragmentation reduced to ~34%, KV hit-rate +6%, p99 improved by ~18% relative to C but not back to B.
E. Batch coalescing heuristic (payload-aware): group requests by effective_seq_len buckets before dynamic-batching (4 buckets), then run C. fragmentation reduced to 18%, throughput +23% vs C, p99 improved substantially.

Interpreting the results:
- Simple routing-only fixes (toggle prefetch) help but do not eliminate the core batching inefficiency.
- Payload-aware batching is the most effective short-term lever: by reducing sequence-length variance within a micro-batch we reduce kernel fragmentation and router stragglers. This is a software-only mitigation that can be rolled out in Dedicated pools first.
- MoE-specific changes are necessary medium-term: more asynchronous expert dispatch, per-expert micro-queues, and reduced router barriers.

Short-term mitigations (can be shipped quickly):
- Implement payload-aware bucketing inside the dynamic-batcher: 4 buckets (<=256, 257-2048, 2049-8192, >8192) with fast path for homogenous batches.
- Enable prefetch-experts by default for MoE routes with long-context flag; add telemetry to detect when prefetch harms throughput so it can be toggled.
- Add a runtime metric: fragmentation_ratio exposed in the console for per-model dashboards to correlate with cost/latency.

Medium-term mitigations (architectural):
- Asynchronous expert dispatch: remove global router barriers; allow experts to process their sub-batches independently, with a barrier only at token-commit if needed. This will require careful memory and KV consistency guarantees.
- KV cache placement stability: move to deterministic placement of KV shards per-request to avoid eviction thrash when batch composition changes.
- Kernel fusion for small scatter/gather ops: fuse repeated small dispatch kernels into fewer larger kernels where possible to reduce launch overhead.

Long-term ideas (research-level):
- Cost-aware routing: incorporate expected effective_seq_len and historical latency into gating decisions so gates prefer experts that minimize combined compute+io cost.
- Hybrid static/dynamic coalescing: offline profiling to compute coalescing strategies per model and per customer workload.

Open questions and follow-ups:
- How does fragmentation behave under multi-card sharding (tensor/pipeline) and for Dedicated pools with 4–8 cards? Need cross-card traces.
- What are the correctness/perf tradeoffs of removing router barriers for top-k gating (especially for MoE models that rely on soft-expert normalize steps)?
- Can we build a cheap online estimator of fragmentation_ratio at the router input to dynamically switch batching strategies?

Action items (owners):
- eng-serving-runtime: implement payload-aware bucketing in the dynamic-batcher prototype (Arjun Patel, due 2026-01-15).
- eng-serving-runtime: prototype async expert dispatch in an isolated branch and simulation harness (Maya Chen, Omar Haddad, due 2026-03-01).
- observability: add fragmentation_ratio and router_sync_wait to per-model dashboards (Lucia Romero, due 2026-02-05).

Appendix: quick repro commands and notes:
- Trace capture: use runtime profile flag --trace-mode=per-step --trace-sample=0.1 --trace-kv to capture router and kv timings.
- Batching debug: set env DEBUG_BATCHER=1 to emit batch composition logs (request ids, effective_seq_len, bucket ids).
- Sizing note: on A100 single-card runs, prefetch adds a steady ~6% memory overhead but improves p99 in 60% of long-context traces.

Closing note:
Payload heterogeneity is a first-class signal for inference platforms. Our experiments show that a small change in batching strategy yields outsized improvements for long-context and MoE mixes. Priorities: ship payload-aware bucketing, add telemetry, and continue the async-expert prototype.
